title: Comments of Crusoe Technologies LLC in response to PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s 60-Day Compliance Filing for Co-Located Load Related Revisions to Open Access Transmission Tariff to Comply with Commission Order under ER26-1479.

documents.name: Crusoe_Comments PJM ER26-1479.pdf
documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                   BEFORE THE
                     FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                                             Docket No. ER26-1479-000


                      COMMENTS OF CRUSOE TECHNOLOGIES LLC

          In accordance with Rules 212 and 213 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s

(Commission) Rules of Practice and Procedure 1 Crusoe Technologies LLC (Crusoe)

respectfully submits these comments in response to PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (PJM) 60-

Day Compliance Filing 2 filed on February 23, 2026 (PJM Compliance Filing). The PJM

Compliance Filing was submitted in response to the Commission’s December 18, 2025 Order

on Show Cause Proceeding, 3 regarding the co-location of large loads in PJM.

I.        SUMMARY OF COMMENTS

          Crusoe appreciates PJM’s efforts to advance large load interconnection and its

thoughtful engagement with stakeholders in developing a workable approach. Crusoe supports

policy efforts that facilitate “bring your own power” frameworks and are built on an energy-

first model that allow co-located generation to enhance grid reliability, reduce ratepayer costs,

and accelerate the buildout of AI infrastructure. Crusoe believes that certain targeted revisions

to PJM’s compliance filing will help ensure the Commission’s December 18 Order achieves its

purpose of enabling large loads to interconnect quickly and reliably while protecting the

transmission system and other ratepayers.


1
    18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212, 385.213 (2025).
2
 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 60-Day Compliance Filing for Co-Located Load Related to Revisions to
Open Access Transmission Tariff to Comply with Commission Order in Docket No. EL25-49, et al.,
FERC Docket No. ER26-1479-000 (Feb. 23, 2026) (PJM Compliance Filing).
3
    PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al., 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 (2025) (December 18 Order).
 Docket No. ER26-1479-000

       First, PJM’s proposed 50 MW materiality threshold for new Retail Behind-the-Meter

Generation (Retail BTMG) is too low and could produce unjust and unreasonable outcomes for

larger co-located loads. The Commission should direct PJM to revise the threshold upward and

calibrate it to the size of the co-located load at the relevant electrical location. Second, while

PJM’s Interim Network Integration Transmission Service (Interim NITS) is a useful tool to

help facilitate large load interconnections, it should be clarified to ensure that co-located

generation is able to supply co-located load during curtailment events, including while the

generator is still being studied in the interconnection process.

       Third, while Crusoe supports PJM’s proposed menu of three new transmission service

options, the Commission should direct PJM to provide clear Tariff procedures for establishing,

adjusting, and terminating Contract Demand quantities over time and clarify how point-to-point

service coordinates with co-location arrangements.

       Finally, a well-designed Necessary Studies process is the cornerstone of a successful

Co-Located Load interconnection framework. The Commission has a clear opportunity to

establish a process that is both expeditious and predictable — one that gives developers the

certainty they need to invest with confidence and move projects forward at the speed the

market demands.

       To realize this opportunity, the Commission should take three affirmative steps. First,

establish binding study timelines with enforceable milestones that bring discipline and

accountability to the review process. Second, focus study scope where it matters most — on

reliability impacts directly attributable to non-exporting resources — ensuring reviews are

targeted, efficient, and technically sound. Third, adopt and publish a clear, transparent standard

for study triggers, giving all stakeholders a common roadmap and eliminating the ambiguity


                                                 2
 Docket No. ER26-1479-000

that slows project development. Together, these measures will transform the Necessary Studies

process into a genuine enabler of Co-Located Load interconnection — providing the speed,

transparency, and reliability that both the Commission and the market need to unlock the full

potential of co-location.

II.    BACKGROUND

       Crusoe is a vertically integrated Artificial Intelligence (AI) infrastructure company that

builds, owns, and operates data centers specifically optimized for the high-performance

computing requirements of AI and machine learning workloads. Crusoe’s “bring your own

power” philosophy is founded on the goal of harnessing stranded and otherwise wasted energy

to power computation. Crusoe's business model is built on an energy-first approach—where

co-located generation, when structured correctly, simultaneously advances grid reliability,

reduces ratepayer costs, and accelerates AI infrastructure. Crusoe appreciates PJM's

engagement with stakeholders on this matter and recognizes that PJM's decisions here may

serve as a national model.

       Crusoe supports the Commission's goal of creating a clear, workable framework with

optionality for interconnecting new large loads embedded in the new transmission service

options. Our goal is speed to power responsibly. Crusoe’s guiding principle is straightforward:

move the compute to the energy, not the other way around. Traditional data center

development follows the grid – waiting for interconnection approvals, straining existing

infrastructure, and too often driving up electricity costs for the communities it enters. Crusoe

takes the opposite approach and instead locates AI workloads near sources of abundant, often

underutilized energy – tapping into places traditional data centers do not reach.




                                                3
 Docket No. ER26-1479-000

       Crusoe's primary operations involve sourcing and developing cost-effective energy,

including natural gas, renewable power (e.g., wind, solar) and battery storage, to power its data

center facilities. Crusoe leverages its in-house manufacturing capabilities to rapidly deploy

computing infrastructure that provides reliable, low-latency cloud services, including access to

leading-edge graphics processing units (GPUs), to enterprise customers and AI developers.

Through its energy-first approach, Crusoe aims to reduce both the cost and the environmental

impact of utility-scale computing infrastructure.

III.   COMMENTS

       A.      PJM’s Proposed 50 MW Materiality Threshold for New Retail BTMG
               Should Be Revised Upward.

       PJM proposes a materiality threshold of up to 50 MW for a new generator to qualify as

Retail BTMG, contending that this threshold corresponds with the PJM Board’s definition of

large load additions (i.e., individual loads of 50 MW or greater at a single point of

interconnection). Crusoe respectfully submits that this threshold is misaligned with the

regulatory purpose it purports to serve and will undermine the very policy goals the

Commission sought to advance in the December 18 Order.

       The 50 MW threshold, while aligned with the PJM Board’s definition of large load

additions, was designed as an administrative planning threshold, not as a bright-line test for

what constitutes a reliability risk. Applying the threshold as the sole determinant of Retail

BTMG eligibility conflates two distinct regulatory purposes. A planning metric developed to

identify large load additions for administrative purposes is not, and should not become, a proxy

for measuring when behind-the-meter generation creates transmission system risk. The

Commission should decline to treat these two distinct purposes as interchangeable.




                                                 4
 Docket No. ER26-1479-000

          Large loads come in many sizes, and co-location arrangements can vary significantly.

The Retail BTMG threshold should be flexible and non-discriminatory to account for these

differences. A fixed 50 MW cap raises serious concerns about disparate treatment of large

loads of different sizes. PJM’s own filing acknowledges that a lower threshold risks forcing

existing BTMG resources offline during the transition period—an outcome that would increase

grid burden, not reduce it, by converting currently netted load into full network load without

corresponding new capacity additions. 4 This outcome warrants careful consideration by the

Commission, as it does not reflect a principled distinction among similarly situated customers.

          Stripping a new large load of netting rights if it has Retail BTMG greater than 50 MW

penalizes the very co-location configurations that can ease grid congestion. BTMG

arrangements can benefit the transmission system in many ways, such as by serving load on a

streamlined basis, avoiding queue delays in the generator interconnection process, and by

reducing the need for expensive grid upgrades. These are not speculative benefits – they are

the precise outcomes the Commission’s bring your own power framework was designed to

produce.

          The optimal sizing of Retail BTMG (such as solar plus battery energy storage systems or

some other combination) to support AI data center would most certainly exceed 50 MW.

Accordingly, Crusoe supports an approach that limits the size of Retail BTMG in proportion to

the size of the load.




4
    PJM Compliance Filing at 12 (Sec. III.A.2.c).

                                                    5
 Docket No. ER26-1479-000

          B.      PJM’s Proposed Interim NITS Framework Must Allow Co-Located
                  Generation and Retail BTMG to Serve Co-Located Load During
                  Curtailment Events on the Grid.

          PJM proposes Interim NITS as a transition service until the transmission system can

support the large load customer’s NITS request. 5 According to PJM, “Interim NITS is

premised on the notion that the Co-Located Load is willing and able to limit its energy

withdrawals from the Transmission System prior to NITS being available. 6 Crusoe supports

Interim NITS as a bridge service where it adds genuine value: the period during which a single

building or phase of a data center campus is coming online while co-locating generation and/or

Retail BTMG is still being built and interconnected. In that context, Interim NITS provides a

workable, near-term solution to allow load to operate on the transmission system.

          PJM’s proposed approach to implementing Interim NITS, however, appears to treat new

Co-Located Generating Facilities as equivalent to full PJM Resources prior to the Co-Located

Generating Facilities receiving firm Network Resource status. It is not clear if PJM intends to

prevent Co-Located Generating Facilities or Retail BTMG from supplying energy to Co-

Located Load during a grid curtailment event if the Co-Located Load is at that time being

served via Interim NITS. If that is PJM’s proposal, it would create a large disincentive to large

load customers from utilizing Interim NITS as an option for speedy interconnection. If large

load customers cannot rely upon their own Co-Located Generating Facilities or Retail BTMG

during the Interim NITS period, it would create a significant disincentive and effectively nullify

Interim NITS as a viable transmission service option and commercial pathway.




5
    Initial Brief of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. EL25-49, at 67 (Feb. 23, 2026) (PJM Brief).
6
    PJM Brief at 71.

                                                     6
 Docket No. ER26-1479-000

          This concern is not unique to Crusoe. Large loads electing to take Interim NITS accept

the risk of grid curtailment, but they should not have to completely shut down during a grid

curtailment if they can rely on co-located generation or Retail BTMG without relying on the

transmission grid. The PJM tariff should allow a Co-Located Generating Facility to serve its

Co-Located Load directly—without grid injection—while still being studied through the

applicable generator interconnection study process.

          C.      PJM’s Proposed Three New Transmission Service Options Should Be
                  Accepted, With Additional Guidance on Contract Demand Procedures.

          Crusoe strongly supports the Commission’s decision to create a menu of transmission

service options. The ability to right-size transmission service to actual grid dependence is a

smart policy approach that aligns cost of transmission service with actual usage. Crusoe

supports PJM’s proposed three new transmission service options that will benefit large load

customers. According to PJM, large load customers will have the option to take a combination

of Firm and Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service, so long as the combined

service fully covers the co-located load's total load. 7 The new transmission service options will

encourage flexible co-location structures that will enable speedy and reliable interconnection

for large loads.

          Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service is the appropriate long-term service for

data centers that have stable, predictable on-site generation and limited grid draw. Non-Firm

Contract Demand provides valuable optionality for sites where grid dependence varies. This is

especially true for Crusoe’s phased campus development model, where generation and load

come online in stages. The three-service menu allows Crusoe to right-size its transmission



7
    Initial Brief of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. EL25-49-000 at 7 (Feb. 23, 2026).

                                                     7
 Docket No. ER26-1479-000

service obligations as each phase matures, avoiding unnecessary costs during buildout while

ensuring the grid is protected at every stage.

       However, the illustrative Tariff language in the PJM Brief leaves certain critical

questions unanswered regarding how the contract demand MW quantity is established and

modified over time. 8 The compliance filing does not (1) explain how the initial contract

demand quantity is determined (i.e., whether by customer request, as determined by study, or

by some other mechanism), (2) address whether contract demand quantities can be adjusted as

load grows in phases or (3) specify how point-to-point transmission service interacts with co-

location arrangements where both generation and load sit on the developer's side of the Point of

Change in Ownership.

       These are important implementation details for a multi-gigawatt campus developer like

Crusoe. An inability to adjust contract demand quantities in step with phased load growth

would require either over-purchasing transmission service in early phases or risk non-

compliance as load grows. The Commission should ensure that the final Tariff language does

not place large load customers in this position by directing PJM to provide detailed procedures

for establishing, adjusting, and terminating Contract Demand quantities, and to clarify how

point-to-point transmission service coordinates with co-location configurations in the final

Tariff language.




8
 PJM Brief, Attachment A, Illustrative Language for New Tariff, Part XI; Attachments F-3A and F-4;
and Other Illustrative Tariff Revisions.


                                                 8
 Docket No. ER26-1479-000

       D.      The Necessary Studies Process Must Be Expeditious and Not Become a
               Barrier to Co-Located Load Development.

       The Necessary Studies process must be fast, predictable, and not become a barrier to

interconnecting new Co-Located Load. A Necessary Studies process that introduces open-

ended timelines, redundant review of generation resources that are not being injected into the

grid, or unclear criteria for what triggers a study will directly undermine this goal. The PJM

Necessary Studies should be designed with stakeholders and practical timelines in mind.

Crusoe recommends a series of workshops with industry to design these timelines. In this

regard, PJM should (1) establish binding timelines for the completion of Necessary Studies

applicable to Co-Located Load; (2) limit the scope of Necessary Studies where new generation

resources are not interconnecting to the transmission system to reliability impacts only; and (3)

create a clear, published standard for what triggers a Necessary Study so that developers can

plan with certainty. Speed and certainty in the Necessary Studies process are not in tension

with reliability, they are prerequisites for delivering the AI infrastructure capacity the nation

requires at the pace the market demands.


IV.    CONCLUSION

       For the reasons discussed above, Crusoe Technologies LLC respectfully urges the

Commission to adopt targeted revisions to PJM’s compliance filing that will facilitate the

reliable and timely interconnection of large loads, support the development of flexible co-

location arrangements, and ensure that necessary studies and tariff procedures do not create

unnecessary barriers for innovative energy-first data center models. By refining the materiality

threshold for Retail BTMG, clarifying the application of Interim NITS, providing detailed

guidance for contract demand procedures, and ensuring an expeditious and transparent studies



                                                 9
 Docket No. ER26-1479-000

process, the Commission can advance its policy objectives while protecting the interests of the

transmission system and ratepayers. Crusoe appreciates the Commission’s and PJM’s ongoing

engagement with stakeholders and looks forward to continued collaboration in building a

robust framework for the next generation of AI infrastructure.
